title: Number of 1 Bits
notes:
Task and constraints: Count set bits in the 32-bit unsigned representation of n.
Idea: Mask n with 0xFFFFFFFF to retain its low 32 bits, then call bit_count on that nonnegative value.
Technique and why it applies: Fixed-width masking makes Python's unbounded signed integer behave like the specified 32-bit bit pattern before counting ones.
Invariant: The masked value has exactly the same low 32 bits as n and no higher bits.
Edge cases: 11 (1011) returns 3; zero returns 0; a negative Python integer is converted to its low 32-bit representation by the mask.
Complexity: Time O(1), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The implementation performs one fixed-width mask and one bit-count operation.

title: Number of 1 Bits
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the number of one bits in the 32-bit representation of n.
Idea: hammingWeight delegates the calculation directly to Integer.bitCount(n).
Technique and why it applies: The JDK intrinsic counts set bits in the primitive int representation without a manual scan.
Invariant: The returned count is the population count of all 32 bits, including the sign bit for negative ints.
Edge cases: 11 returns 3; zero returns 0; a negative int is treated as its two's-complement 32-bit pattern.
Complexity: Time O(1), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The method calls Integer.bitCount once and allocates no data structure.

title: House Robber
notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize robbed value from nonnegative linearly arranged houses without choosing adjacent houses.
Idea: Keep two_back and one_back as the best totals two and one positions behind; for each amount, shift the states and choose between skipping it and adding it to two_back.
Technique and why it applies: Rolling dynamic programming retains only the two predecessor states required by the recurrence.
Invariant: After each house, one_back is the optimum for the processed prefix and two_back is the optimum for the prefix excluding its last house.
Edge cases: Empty input returns 0; [2,7,9,3,1] returns 12; a single house returns its amount.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop processes each house once and stores two totals.

title: House Robber
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the maximum sum from nonadjacent houses with nonnegative values.
Idea: For each amount compute best=max(oneBack,twoBack+amount), then shift oneBack into twoBack and best into oneBack.
Technique and why it applies: The recurrence compares skipping the current house with robbing it after the best prefix ending two houses earlier.
Invariant: oneBack is the optimal total through the previous house, while twoBack is the optimal total through the house before that.
Edge cases: Empty array returns 0; the sample returns 12; one house returns its value. Java int totals assume the problem's bounds avoid overflow.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The enhanced for loop visits each array entry once and uses three integer state variables.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the rightmost node value at each level of a binary tree, top to bottom.
Idea: Return [] for null root; otherwise BFS with deque, freeze level_size, enqueue children, and append node.val when i is the last index of that level.
Technique and why it applies: Level-order traversal groups nodes by depth, and the last dequeued node in each group is visible from the right.
Invariant: At each inner-loop start, the next level_size queue entries are exactly the current level.
Edge cases: Null root returns []; a single node returns its value; in [1,2,3,null,5,null,4], the result is [1,3,4].
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(w) for maximum queue width.
complexity_reason: Each node is enqueued and dequeued once, and the queue holds at most one or two adjacent levels' frontier.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
notes:
Task and constraints: Produce the right-side view of a binary tree, listing one visible value per depth.
Idea: Use an ArrayDeque queue, capture queue.size() as levelSize, process exactly that many nodes, enqueue children, and append the last node's value.
Technique and why it applies: BFS visits each depth in order, making its final processed node the rightmost node at that level.
Invariant: Nodes added while processing a level are reserved for the next outer iteration because levelSize is fixed.
Edge cases: Null root returns an empty list; one node yields one value; the example tree yields [1,3,4]. ArrayDeque disallows null entries, and only non-null children are offered.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(w).
complexity_reason: Each tree node enters and leaves the queue once, with queue size bounded by the maximum level width.

title: Number of Islands
notes:
Task and constraints: Count four-directionally connected land components in a grid, including isolated '1' cells.
Idea: Scan every cell; when a '1' appears, increment islands, mark it '0', and use a stack to visit and mark all adjacent land before continuing the scan.
Technique and why it applies: Iterative flood fill explores an entire connected component once and mutates visited cells to prevent recounting.
Invariant: Every cell pushed on the stack is land already changed to water, so no cell is scheduled twice.
Edge cases: Empty grid or empty first row returns 0; the example connected block counts as one; diagonal-only land cells count as separate islands. The input grid is modified.
Complexity: Time O(rows*cols), space O(rows*cols) worst case.
complexity_reason: The outer scan visits every cell and the stack can hold a component's cells.

title: Number of Islands
notes:
Task and constraints: Count connected groups of '1' cells using only horizontal and vertical neighbors.
Idea: Scan the char matrix; for each unseen land cell increment islands, push its coordinates, mark it water, then iteratively pop cells and inspect four directions.
Technique and why it applies: Flood fill visits every member of a component and marks it on insertion so components are counted once.
Invariant: Any cell already placed on the stack has been changed to '0', preventing duplicate pushes.
Edge cases: Zero rows or columns returns 0; diagonal contact does not connect islands; the method changes the input grid. The per-pop directions array is repeatedly allocated in this implementation.
Complexity: Time O(rows*cols), space O(rows*cols).
complexity_reason: Every cell is marked and processed at most once, and the explicit stack can grow to the number of land cells.

title: Bitwise AND of Numbers Range
notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the bitwise AND of every integer in inclusive [left,right].
Idea: Shift both bounds right together until equal, counting shifts, then shift the common prefix left by the same amount.
Technique and why it applies: Any bit position that changes among numbers in the interval becomes zero in their AND; the remaining common high-order prefix is preserved.
Invariant: After each shift, left and right are the original endpoints with the same number of low bits removed.
Edge cases: [5,7] returns 4; equal endpoints return that number without shifting; intervals spanning a power-of-two boundary lose the differing lower bits.
Complexity: Time O(log right), space O(1).
complexity_reason: Each loop removes one low bit from both bounds and increments a single counter.

title: Bitwise AND of Numbers Range
notes:
Task and constraints: AND all integers from left through right inclusive.
Idea: While left<right, unsigned-shift both endpoints and increment shifts; once equal, restore their common prefix by shifting it left.
Technique and why it applies: The answer is the shared high-bit prefix because every bit position varying across the range is cleared by AND.
Invariant: Both bounds have been shifted equally, preserving the common prefix that can survive the full-range AND.
Edge cases: [5,7] returns 4; equal bounds return unchanged; unsigned >>> prevents sign extension for high-bit-set ints. Left shifting the prefix reconstructs the surviving bits.
Complexity: Time O(log right), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop shifts two integers until they converge and stores one shift count.

title: Happy Number
approach_name: Floyd cycle detection on digit transforms
notes:
Task and constraints: Decide whether repeated digit-square sums reach 1 or enter a non-1 cycle.
Idea: digit_square_sum extracts decimal digits with divmod and sums their squares; slow advances once and fast twice until fast is 1 or both pointers meet.
Technique and why it applies: Floyd cycle detection identifies a repeating transformation sequence without storing every prior number.
Invariant: slow and fast remain positions in the same deterministic sequence, with fast moving twice as quickly.
Edge cases: 19 returns true; 2 enters a non-1 cycle and returns false; zero maps to zero and returns false. The helper returns zero for value zero.
Complexity: Time is O(d*t) for d digits processed across t transformations; space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each transformation scans the current number's decimal digits, while slow and fast use constant storage.

title: Happy Number
approach_name: Floyd cycle detection on digit transforms
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if repeated sums of squared decimal digits reach 1, false if they cycle elsewhere.
Idea: digitSquareSum repeatedly extracts n%10, accumulates digit*digit, and divides by ten; isHappy advances slow once and fast twice.
Technique and why it applies: Floyd's tortoise-hare algorithm detects a cycle in the deterministic sequence with constant memory.
Invariant: Both pointers follow the same transformation, and equality before reaching 1 proves the sequence is cycling.
Edge cases: 19 reaches 1; 2 cycles and returns false; zero returns false. The helper assumes nonnegative input because its loop condition is n>0.
Complexity: Time depends on transformations and digits per transform; space O(1).
complexity_reason: The digit helper scans each decimal digit and the main method stores only two pointers.

title: Remove Linked List Elements
notes:
Task and constraints: Remove every linked-list node equal to val, including matches at the head.
Idea: Place dummy before head and keep current at dummy; inspect current.next, bypass it when its value matches, otherwise advance current.
Technique and why it applies: A dummy predecessor lets the same link-update rule remove both the original head and interior nodes.
Invariant: All nodes before current.next have been checked and retained only if their value differs from val.
Edge cases: Empty list returns None; [6,6] removes all nodes; consecutive matches are handled because current does not advance after bypassing a node.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The pointer advances over each retained node and bypasses each removed node without allocating a replacement list.

title: Remove Linked List Elements
notes:
Task and constraints: Delete all nodes with value val from a singly linked list and return the possibly new head.
Idea: Create dummy with next=head; inspect current.next until null, bypass matches by assigning next.next, otherwise advance current, then return dummy.next.
Technique and why it applies: The dummy node provides a predecessor even when the first several original nodes must be deleted.
Invariant: Nodes already passed remain linked in the result only when their values differ from val.
Edge cases: Null head returns null; repeated head matches are removed in place; the final node is handled when current.next becomes null. The dummy node is an extra constant-size allocation.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop visits each original node once and changes only next pointers.

title: Count Primes
notes:
Task and constraints: Count primes strictly below n; marking multiples is more efficient than trial-dividing every integer.
Idea: Return zero for n<=2, initialize a bytearray, clear indices 0 and 1, and for each prime p through sqrt(n-1) zero its multiples starting at p*p using slice assignment.
Technique and why it applies: The Sieve of Eratosthenes marks composites once per prime factor, starting at p squared because smaller multiples were handled earlier.
Invariant: Before processing p, every unmarked value at least two is prime; marking p's multiples removes composites.
Edge cases: n=2 returns 0; n=10 returns 4; starting at p*p preserves p itself. Slice assignment's count is computed to fit indices below n.
Complexity: O(n log log n) time, O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The sieve stores n flags and marks each composite through prime-multiple slices.

title: Count Primes
notes:
Task and constraints: Count primes less than n with the Sieve of Eratosthenes.
Idea: Initialize boolean isPrime, clear 0 and 1, mark multiples of each surviving p starting at p*p while p*p<n, then count true entries.
Technique and why it applies: Composite numbers have a prime factor no larger than their square root, so marking from p squared eliminates every composite below n.
Invariant: When p is reached, any composite multiple below p*p was already marked by a smaller prime.
Edge cases: n<=2 returns 0; n=10 counts 2,3,5,7; p*p uses int multiplication, which can overflow for extremely large n beyond practical array sizes.
Complexity: O(n log log n) time, O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The boolean array has n entries, and the sieve plus final count scans those entries and their multiples.

title: Isomorphic Strings
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether equal-length strings admit a one-to-one character mapping from s to t.
Idea: Reject unequal lengths, then compare the number of distinct (source,target) pairs with the distinct source and target character counts.
Technique and why it applies: Equal cardinalities of zipped pairs and both alphabets ensure neither one source maps to multiple targets nor multiple sources map to one target.
Invariant: Each zipped pair records the mapping observed at one position, and set cardinalities measure unique pairs and characters.
Edge cases: "egg"/"add" returns true; "foo"/"bar" returns false; two empty strings return true. Python's Unicode characters are compared as string elements.
Complexity: Expected O(n) time and O(n) space for the sets.
complexity_reason: The zip traversal builds sets of pairs and characters, each with at most n entries.

title: Isomorphic Strings
notes:
Task and constraints: Check whether two equal-length strings have a bijective character mapping.
Idea: Allocate sourceToTarget and targetToSource arrays indexed by UTF-16 char; at each i compare their last-seen indices, then set both entries to i+1.
Technique and why it applies: Matching last-seen positions detects both conflicting directions without hash maps.
Invariant: For each character seen so far, its mapping partner must have exactly the same previous occurrence index.
Edge cases: "egg"/"add" returns true; "foo"/"bar" fails when o would map to both a and r; empty strings return true. Arrays cover all char values and use fixed-size space.
Complexity: Time O(n), auxiliary space O(1) with respect to input length.
complexity_reason: The loop visits n UTF-16 code units and accesses two fixed 65,536-entry arrays.

title: Reverse Linked List
notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse a singly linked list in place and return the new head.
Idea: Track previous and current; save current.next in following, point current.next backward, then advance both pointers until current is None.
Technique and why it applies: Iterative pointer reversal changes each link once while following retains access to the unprocessed suffix.
Invariant: previous is the head of the reversed prefix, while current heads the untouched suffix.
Edge cases: None returns None; a singleton returns itself; [1,2,3] becomes [3,2,1]. Saving following before rewiring prevents losing the remaining nodes.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop visits every node once and maintains three node references.

title: Reverse Linked List
notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse every next link of a singly linked list and return the last original node as head.
Idea: Before changing current.next, save it as following; point current to previous, then advance previous and current until null.
Technique and why it applies: Iterative reversal redirects links from front to back while the saved pointer preserves the remaining chain.
Invariant: previous points to the already reversed prefix and current to the first not-yet-rewired node.
Edge cases: Null head returns null; one node is unchanged; multiple nodes reverse correctly because following is captured before assignment. Java references are updated without allocating new list nodes.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: Each node is processed once with a fixed number of reference assignments and no auxiliary collection.
